claims.text: The 429 status code indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time, which the specification glosses as rate limiting. Response representations SHOULD include details explaining the condition, and MAY include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait before making a new request.

source.title: RFC 6585, Additional HTTP Status Codes, M. Nottingham and R. Fielding, April 2012

claims.text: The specification is explicit about what it does not standardise: it does not define how the origin server identifies the user, nor how it counts requests. An origin server limiting request rates can do so based upon counts of requests on a per-resource basis, across the entire server, or even among a set of servers.

source.title: RFC 6585, Additional HTTP Status Codes, M. Nottingham and R. Fielding, April 2012

claims.text: The mechanism for telling a client when to come back is defined separately: servers send the Retry-After header field to indicate how long the user agent ought to wait before making a follow-up request, and its value can be either a date or a number of seconds.

source.title: RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, STD 97, R. Fielding, M. Nottingham and J. Reschke eds., June 2022

beats.broke: demand arrives faster than a system can serve it, and a system with no way to refuse work accepts everything, queues without bound, and fails for everybody rather than for the excess
beats.fix: refuse deliberately above a stated rate, telling the caller that it was refused for that reason and when to return, so that the load which cannot be served is shed rather than absorbed
beats.cost: the status code is standardised and the policy is not — who counts as a user, what is counted, and over what window are all yours to define, and every choice is a way of being unfair to somebody
beats.interview: why a system under too much load should reject work rather than queue it
